groundTruthNarrative: In week 31 the General Manager's own cost change (CR-2231) cut the night receiving team from six to four operatives. Inbound volume and slots did not change. Night-received chilled pallets now wait a median of almost four hours on unrefrigerated dock lanes at 15–17°C before put-away, against about 40 minutes before; day receiving is unchanged. Operatives key the 'receiving' probe at the receipt-confirmation step, which in practice happens at put-away. So the 6.6–7.9°C readings the GM cites measure product that has already warmed on the dock, not product as it arrived. Independent trailer telematics show Haverlow loads arriving at 2–3.5°C with no change since July. Haverlow is over-represented in write-offs only because it delivers nights only. Night-received Pellridge and own-label product spoils at the same rate, and day-received product from the same suppliers, stored in the same chambers, does not. The chambers hold temperature. Corriebank's self-certified credit policy coincides with a rise in customer credits, but no evidence separates over-claiming from genuinely shortened shelf life, so that question stays open. The fix is to restore night put-away capacity and cap dock-to-chamber time. The chargeback would punish a supplier that did nothing wrong and would not stop the losses.

answers.rationale: The GM's claim rests on E3, the DC's own probe entries. C6 is unit-logged, uneditable trailer telematics, pulled by Tallowmere's own planner from a haulier that also serves Tallowmere's outbound fleet. It shows every Haverlow load at 1.9–3.6°C return air and 2.4–3.5°C product probe at door-open, with no trend since July. C11 adds that Haverlow's night write-off rate equals that of other night-received suppliers. E4 and C1 are consistent with this but come from an interested party.

C6 shows product arriving at about 3°C and trailers emptied by around 23:20. E3 shows the same loads reading 6.6–7.9°C when confirmed at about 02:30–03:20. C11 shows night pallets sitting a median of 3 h 52 min on unrefrigerated dock lanes at 15–17°C, and night-received product written off at 2.9% against 0.6% for day-received product. Initial file alone cannot establish this.

E6 shows the chambers at 1.7–3.9°C, with calibrated probes and the normal alarm count. C11 shows day-received product put into the same CH1–CH3 chambers keeping a 0.5–0.6% write-off rate, which a chamber fault would not allow. The GM is right on this point; his error lies elsewhere.

E3's header says the probe is taken at unload, but C6 puts door-open at 22:18–23:06 and the trailers empty by 22:55–23:47. Receipt confirmation, where the temperature is keyed, comes 3.5–4 hours later. Product at 2.4–3.5°C at door-open cannot be the 6.6–7.9°C product recorded, so the entries do not reflect condition off the trailer. Only C6 supplies the door-open times.

E7 gives a plausible opportunity and a rise in Corriebank credits, but only anecdotal suspicion. C11 explicitly excludes customer credits because they cannot be traced to a receiving shift. No item tests claim validity, and genuine shelf-life loss from dock warming is an equally live explanation.

E5 cuts the night crew only, from week 31, with slots unchanged. C11 shows night dock-to-chamber time stepping from 44 min to 3 h 05 min in week 31 and 3 h 52 min afterwards. Night volume is flat (118 to 121 pallets) and day receiving, with an unchanged crew, stays at about 40 min. Temporal order, mechanism and a within-site comparison that rules out a volume rise together establish causation.

C11 traces lots to receiving shift. Night-received write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%; day-received stayed at 0.6% for the same suppliers (Pellridge, own-label) and the same chambers. That rules out supplier and storage rivals. The mechanism is unrefrigerated dock lanes at 15–17°C for about four hours, consistent with the warm probe readings in E3. C6 independently removes arrival temperature as a rival.

The link itself fails. C6 shows Haverlow arrival temperatures unchanged and within spec on every load before and during the spike, so arrival temperature cannot have driven the increase. C11 shows Haverlow's write-off rate matching other night-received suppliers. Its large share in E1 reflects night-only delivery, not arrival condition.

The policy started on 3 August, and Corriebank credits rose from about £1,250 to £3,100 a week at the same time (E7; E1 totals). That shows co-occurrence. However, dock warming began in the same weeks and would genuinely shorten shelf life at stores (C11, C4). No customer comparison or claim-level validation separates the two, so causation is not established.

Independent telematics clear Haverlow, so the chargeback punishes the wrong party. Moving volume to Pellridge fixes nothing, because Pellridge's night-received product spoils at the same rate. It also adds 4–6% cost and possible capacity fees (C15, C8). This holds whether or not the live rival H5 is true, because over-claiming would not implicate Haverlow either.

It directly reverses the established cause, the night crew cut that produced long dock times and spoilage. It costs about £2,300 a week (E5) against a roughly £15,700 a week rise in DC-stage write-offs (E1), and it builds in monitoring. It is the single action addressing the confirmed, larger driver, and it helps whatever the answer on H5.

If over-claiming were confirmed, reinstating photo evidence would clearly help, and asking for it does little lasting damage if wrong. However, its stated basis (H5) is unestablished. The credit rise co-occurs with genuine dock warming, so committing now is not justified.

Reconciling claims is a reasonable, low-cost way to test H5 on the smaller credit component (about £2,700 a week of the rise). It does not address the established and larger DC-stage driver, so it is not the action that should lead.
It removes the only check that would detect warm product. It would hide the dock-warming signal, and it would also hide any real supplier excursion. It worsens outcomes under every live hypothesis.

With C6 and C11, the chain from crew cut to dock time to warming to write-offs is established. The supplier and chamber rivals are excluded, and the action is cheap and reversible relative to the losses. The open question on credit claims (H5) does not bear on whether to restore night put-away capacity.

authoringNotes: Interested party: the GM, who sponsored CR-2231 and claims it had no service impact. He builds his supplier-blame case on the DC's own probe entries (E3) and a chamber dashboard (E6) that is accurate but irrelevant. Independent record: Haverlow's trailer telematics (C6), which are unit-logged, uneditable and pulled by Tallowmere's own staff. They contradict the claim of warm arrivals and expose the timing of the probe entries. Confound: Haverlow delivers nights only, so supplier identity tracks receiving shift. C11 breaks this by comparing the same suppliers and chambers across shifts. Non-redundancy: only C6 settles H4, because it alone gives door-open times to set against E3's confirmation times. It also gives the decisive independent evidence on H1 and R3. Only C11 settles R1, R2, A2 and SUFF, because it alone gives dock times, shift-level write-off rates and the dock temperature. No other catalogue item reports arrival times, dock dwell or shift-level spoilage. C1 is the accused supplier's own dispatch data and does not cover arrival. C2 and C12 confirm points already settled. C3 cannot locate the abuse. C13 restates E7. Initial-file traps: E3's SOP header ('probe at unload'), the 58% Haverlow share, and E6's clean chambers all point to the supplier. Fair counter-signals in the initial file: other suppliers are also up (E1), Haverlow's denial (E4), the timing of CR-2231 (E5), the note that probes are keyed at receipt confirmation (E3), and the dock lying outside the dashboard (E6). H5 and R4 are deliberately left unresolved by every catalogue item, because credits are excluded from the shift tracing in C11. Only A2 is preferred; the case asks for the single leading action.
